'''vorticose''' (vôr′ti-kōs), ''a.'' [< L. ''vortex'' (''vortic-''), a whirl, vortex, + ''-ose''.] '''1.''' Whirling; vortical.
{{smaller block|Only a very small percentage of the spots show any trace of ''vorticose'' motion. {{right|''C. A. Young'', The Sun, p. 173.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''anat.'', specifying the veins of the external layer of the choroid coat of the eyeball, the venæ vorticosæ, which are regularly arranged in drooping branches converging to a few equidistant trunks which perforate the sclerotic coat and empty into the ophthalmic vein.

{{smaller block|<poem>The fix’d and rooted earth,
Tormented into billows, heaves and swells,
Or with ''vortiginous'' and hideous whirl
Sucks down its prey insatiable.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, ii. 102.}}}}

'''votal''' (vō′tạl), ''a.'' [< L. ''votum'', a vow, + ''-al.''] Pertaining to a vow or promise; consisting in or involving a promise. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Debt is not deadly sin when a man hath no means, but when he hath no meaning to pay. There must be ''votal'' restitution, if there cannot be actual.
{{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 145.}}}}

'''votaress''' (vō′ta̤-res), ''n.'' [< ''votar-y'' + ''-ess.''] A female votary.
{{smaller block|<poem>His woeful queen we leave at Ephesus,
Unto Diana there a ''votaress.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, Prol., iv.}}}}

'''votarist''' (vō′tạ-rist), ''n.'' [< ''votar-y'' + ''-ist.''] A votary.
{{smaller block|The ''votarists'' of Saint Clare. ''Shak.'', M. for M., i. 4. 5.
<poem>Like a sad ''votarist'' in palmer’s weed.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 189.}}}}

'''votary''' (vō′tạ-ri), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< NL. *''votarius'', < L. ''votum'', a vow: see ''vote'', ''vow.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' Consecrated by a vow or promise; also, consequent on a vow; devoted; votive.
{{smaller block|''Votary'' resolution is made equipollent to custom, even in matter of blood.
{{right|''Bacon'', Custom and Education (ed. 1887), p. 397.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.''; pl. ''votaries'' (-riz). One who is devoted, consecrated, or engaged by a vow or promise; hence, more generally, one who is devoted,

'''vote''' (vōt), ''n.''   [< F. ''vote'', a vote, = Sp. Pg. It. ''voto'', a vow, wish, vote, < L. ''votum'', a promise, wish, an engagement, < ''vovere'', pp. ''votus'', promise, dedicate, vow, wish: see ''vow''.]   '''1†.''' An ardent wish or desire; a prayer; a vow.
{{smaller block|<poem>All the heavens consent
With harmony to tune their notes,
In answer to the public ''votes'',

{{right|''B. Jonson'', Fortunate Isles.}}
''Iol.'' The end of my

''Sev.'' I join with you

Those interchangeable ''votes'' of priest and people, . . . “O Lord, arise, help us, and deliver us for thy Name’s sake! O God, we have heard with our ears, &c.”
{{right|''Prideaux'', Euchologia, p. 226.}}}}
'''2.''' A suffrage; the formal expression of a will, preference, wish, or choice in regard to any measure proposed, in which the person voting has an interest in common with others, either in electing a person to fill a certain situation or office, or in passing laws, rules, regulations, etc. {{smaller|This vote or choice may be expressed by holding up the hand, by standing up, by the voice (''viva voce''), by ballot, or otherwise.}}
{{smaller block|Each party gaped, and looked alternately for their ''vote'' almost to the end of their speeches.
{{right|''Burke'', American Taxation.}}}}
{{smaller block|He . . . was already a forty-shilling freeholder, and was conscious of a ''vote'' for the county.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, xi.}}}}
Hence—'''3.''' That by which will or preference is expressed in elections; a ballot, a ticket, etc.: as, a written ''vote''.
{{smaller block|<poem>The freeman, casting with unpurchased hand
The ''vote'' that shakes the turrets of the land.</poem>
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Poetry, A Metrical Essay.}}}}
'''4.''' That which is allowed, conveyed, or bestowed by the will of a majority; a thing conferred by vote; a grant: as, the ministry received a ''vote'' of confidence; the ''vote'' for the civil service amounted to $24,000,000.—'''5.''' Expression of will by a majority; decision by some expression of the minds of a number; result of voting: as, the ''vote'' was unanimous; the ''vote'' was close.—'''6.''' Votes collectively: as, a movement to capture the labor ''vote''.—{{smaller|'''Casting vote.''' See ''casting-vote.''—'''Cumulative vote.''' See ''cumulative system of voting'', under ''cumulative.''—'''Limited vote''', a form of voting by which the elector is restricted to a less number of votes than there are vacancies, as in the case of a three-cornered constituency (which see, under ''three-cornered'').—'''Straw vote.''' See ''straw''<sup>1</sup>.—'''The floating vote.''' See ''floating''.—'''To split one’s votes.''' See ''split''.}}

'''vote''' (vōt), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''voted'', ppr. ''voting''.   [< F. ''voter'', vote, < ''vote'', vote: see ''vote'', ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To give a vote; formally to express or signify the mind, will, or choice in electing persons to office, or in passing laws, regulations, and the like, or in deciding as to any measure in which one has an interest in common with others.
{{smaller block|<poem>They ''voted'' then to do a deed
As kirkmen to devise.</poem>
{{right|''Battle of Balrinnes'' (Child’s Ballads, VII. 221).}}}}
{{smaller block|For their want of intimate knowledge of affairs, I do not think this ought to disqualify them [women] from ''voting'' at any town-meeting which I ever attended.
{{right|''Emerson'', Woman.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Cumulative system of voting.''' See ''cumulative''.—'''To vote straight,''' to vote the entire ticket, as of a political party, without scratching. [Colloq.] .}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To enact or establish by vote, as a resolution or an amendment.—'''2.''' To grant by vote, as an appropriation.
{{smaller block|Parliament ''voted'' them a hundred thousand pounds.
{{right|''Swift.''}}}}
'''3.''' To declare by general consent; characterize by expression of opinion: as, they ''voted'' the trip a failure. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|It has come to be ''voted'' rather a vulgar thing to be married by banns at all.
{{right|''Daily Telegraph'', March 20, 1888. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

{{smaller|'''To vote down,''' to defeat (a proposition), as in a legislative body; give public judgment against; hence, to put an end to.}}
{{smaller block|Old truths ''voted down'' begin to resume their places.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Christ. Mor., ii. 5.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
